summary: Teaching crowds beyond the Jordan, Jesus is tested by Pharisees about divorce and takes them back to creation, where God made husband and wife one flesh.
key_insight: The Pharisees asked what Moses allowed. Jesus went back further than Moses, to “the beginning,” and spoke of what God intended. Moses’ certificate dealt with hard hearts; it was never God’s design for marriage.
story: Jesus departed from Galilee {Mt} and came to the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Great multitudes followed Him, and He healed them there. {Mt} As He was accustomed, He taught them again. {Mk}
Pharisees came to Him, testing Him: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for just any reason?” {Mt}
He asked them, “What did Moses command you?” They said, “Moses permitted a man to write a certificate of divorce, and to dismiss her.” {Mk}

Jesus answered, “Have you not read that He who made them at the beginning ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? So then, they are no longer two but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let not man separate.” {Mt}

“Why then did Moses command to give a certificate of divorce, and to put her away?” they asked. Jesus said, “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. And I say to you, whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery.” {Mt}

Later, in the house, the disciples asked Him again about this. He told them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her. And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” {Mk}

The disciples said, “If such is the case of the man with his wife, it is better not to marry.” Jesus answered, “All cannot accept this saying, but only those to whom it has been given.” Some are eunuchs from birth, some were made so by men, and some have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake. “He who is able to accept it, let him accept it.” {Mt}
differences: Matthew says Jesus “departed from Galilee” and healed the multitudes; Mark says He “arose from there” and taught them, “as He was accustomed.”

Matthew’s question asks about divorce “for just any reason,” and only Matthew records the words “except for sexual immorality”; Mark’s question asks simply whether divorce is lawful, and his account gives no exception.
In Mark, Jesus first asks what Moses commanded and the Pharisees cite Moses; in Matthew, they raise Moses as an objection after Jesus quotes Genesis.
In Matthew, Jesus gives the ruling to the Pharisees; in Mark, He gives it to the disciples in the house and adds the case of a wife who divorces her husband.
Only Matthew records the disciples’ reaction and Jesus’ words about eunuchs.

fit.question: Matthew says Jesus left Galilee “when Jesus had finished these sayings,” the teaching he sets in Capernaum (Matthew 18; events 89–90). Yet John and Luke tell of months in between: the Feasts of Tabernacles and Dedication, the raising of Lazarus, the stay at Ephraim. Did Matthew skip them?

points.label: A closing formula
points.text: Matthew uses nearly the same words to close each of his five great blocks of teaching (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). The phrase marks the end of a section, not the next day. Matthew tells of no feast that Jesus attended in Jerusalem before the last week, so he passes from the last teaching in Galilee straight to the last journey. Mark, who says only that Jesus “arose from there” (from Capernaum, 9:33), passes over the same months.

points.label: The last leaving of Galilee
points.text: Luke has Jesus, on His way to Jerusalem, passing “through the midst of Samaria and Galilee” (17:11; event 117). McGarvey takes this as the road from Ephraim to the border of Galilee, and Matthew’s “departed from Galilee” as the final leaving; he suggests Matthew’s one sentence takes in both departures, the autumn one and this one. The Gospels record no return to Galilee until after Jesus was risen (Matthew 28:16).

fit.note: Matthew tells what happened without claiming to tell everything in between; leaving events out is not putting them in the wrong order.
fit.short: Matthew passes over the months John and Luke describe; his formula closes a block of teaching, and this was Jesus’ last departure from Galilee.

fit.question: Mark records Jesus’ words with no exception: whoever divorces and remarries commits adultery. Matthew includes “except for sexual immorality.” Did Jesus allow an exception or not?

points.label: Answering the question asked
points.text: The Pharisees asked about divorce “for just any reason,” the very point the rabbis debated. Matthew records Jesus’ full answer to that question: not for any reason, but only for sexual immorality. He records the same exception in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:32).

points.label: A rule everyone understood
points.text: The Law punished adultery with death (Deuteronomy 22:22), and Jewish teachers held that adultery required a husband to divorce his wife. Mark and Luke (Luke 16:18) state the general rule; their first readers would not have read it as forbidding divorce after adultery.

fit.note: Matthew and Mark report one teaching at different lengths; leaving out an exception is not the same as denying it.
fit.short: Matthew records the exception Jesus gave to the Pharisees’ question; Mark states the general rule. Both teach that God intends marriage to last.

fit.question: If the exception is part of Jesus’ teaching, how far does it reach? Does it allow divorce only, or remarriage too?

points.label: Divorce and remarriage permitted
points.text: Many evangelicals hold that sexual unfaithfulness permits, but does not require, the wronged spouse to divorce and remarry. Many also see a second case in Paul’s words about an unbelieving spouse who leaves (1 Corinthians 7:15).

points.label: Divorce, but not remarriage
points.text: Others hold that the exception allows a separation or divorce but not remarriage while the former spouse lives, pointing to the unqualified words in Mark and Luke and to 1 Corinthians 7:10–11.

points.label: A narrower meaning
points.text: Others read “sexual immorality” more narrowly, as unfaithfulness during betrothal (as when Joseph planned to put Mary away, Matthew 1:19) or as marriages the Law forbade (Leviticus 18). On this view Jesus allowed no divorce of a valid marriage.

fit.note: Faithful believers who agree that God designed marriage for life still differ on how far the exception reaches; the words of the Gospels themselves are not in question.
fit.short: Many evangelicals see unfaithfulness as a ground for divorce and remarriage; others allow divorce without remarriage, or read the exception more narrowly.

scene.label: Two schools
scene.text: Deuteronomy 24:1 lets a man divorce his wife if he finds “some uncleanness in her.” The rabbis argued over what that meant. The school of Shammai limited it to sexual sin; the school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost anything, even, as later recorded, for spoiling a meal. The Pharisees’ “for just any reason” came straight from that debate.

scene.label: The certificate
scene.text: The certificate of divorce protected the woman. It proved she was free and could marry again without being charged with adultery. Moses regulated a practice already present; he did not create it (Deuteronomy 24:1–4).

scene.label: Beyond the Jordan
scene.text: Matthew and Mark mean the land east of the river opposite Judea, called Perea, on the pilgrim road down the Jordan valley to Jericho. It belonged to Herod Antipas. John the Baptist had been imprisoned and beheaded for telling Herod that his marriage to Herodias, his brother’s wife, was unlawful (Mark 6:17–18). A public answer about divorce here was not a safe one.

scene.label: A wife who divorces
scene.text: Under Jewish law the right to divorce belonged to the husband. Under Greek and Roman law a wife could divorce her husband too, and Josephus says Herodias left her first husband in defiance of Jewish law. Mark, probably writing for readers in Rome, records Jesus’ word for both.

scene.label: Eunuchs
scene.text: Eunuchs could not marry or father children. Isaiah promised faithful eunuchs “a place and a name Better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5). Some, Jesus says, give up marriage for the sake of the kingdom; Paul was one (1 Corinthians 7:7–8).

witnesses.matthew: Marks the departure from Galilee and notes that Jesus healed the great multitudes who followed Him. Matthew then gives the fuller exchange: the Pharisees’ “for just any reason,” the exception, and the disciples’ startled reply. His Jewish readers knew the rabbis’ debate, and he shows the King answering it from creation itself.
witnesses.mark: Opens with Jesus teaching the gathered crowds “as He was accustomed,” then is brief and absolute. Jesus raises Moses first, then takes the Pharisees past Moses to “the beginning of the creation.” In the house He applies the rule to wives as well as husbands, a word for readers who lived under Roman law.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the Lord of creation, with authority above Moses. He takes marriage back to God’s first design and protects the wife who could be sent away “for just any reason.”
seeing.living: Jesus honors marriage as God’s own joining, not a contract to end when it stops pleasing us. For the married, that is a call to guard what God has joined. For those whose marriages have broken, often through no choice of their own, the Lord who set this standard is also the Lord who bore the sin and the sorrow of all who fall short of it.
seeing.ponder: Do you think of marriage first as what you are permitted to do, or as what God has joined?

preaching.big_idea: The Pharisees asked how a marriage may end; Jesus answered with how God began it.
outline: A high calling and a gift (10–12)
preaching.watch_for: “The beginning” is the key phrase (vv. 4, 8). Jesus does not argue inside the Pharisees’ debate over Deuteronomy 24; He goes behind it to Genesis 1:27 and 2:24.
